flawed_step: Step 3: the claim that once an arc is saturated, no later augmentation can use it again. A later augmentation along the reverse arc restores its residual capacity, so the same arc can be the bottleneck many times.
counterexample: Nodes s,a,b,t, with arcs s->a (C), s->b (C), a->b (1), a->t (C), b->t (C), so m=5. Take C=100. Alternate the paths s-a-b-t (bottleneck 1, saturates a->b) and s-b-a-t (uses the reverse arc b->a, bottleneck 1, restores a->b). Each augmentation adds 1 unit of flow, and the max flow is 2C=200. So this choice of paths takes 200 > 5 iterations.
assessment_summary:
Attempted proof, with a judgment on each step:
1. Each augmentation adds its bottleneck value (a positive integer) to the flow, and residual capacities stay integers. JUSTIFIED: integers are closed under subtraction.
2. Each augmentation makes at least one arc of the path (the bottleneck arc) reach zero residual capacity. JUSTIFIED: this follows from the definition of the bottleneck.
3. A saturated arc never becomes usable again, so each of the m arcs can be the bottleneck at most once. NOT JUSTIFIED: augmenting along the reverse arc v->u gives u->v positive residual capacity again. The definitions say reverse arcs may be used.
4. So the number of iterations is at most m. NOT JUSTIFIED: this depends on step 3. Reverse arcs also mean residual arcs are not limited to the m original edges.
5. So the statement holds for every choice of paths. NOT JUSTIFIED: this depends on steps 3 and 4.

Why the statement is false: in the network above (m=5, C=100), alternating s-a-b-t and s-b-a-t makes each augmentation carry only 1 unit. Check: after s-a-b-t, arc a->b is full and the reverse arc b->a has capacity 1. Path s-b-a-t then has bottleneck min(C,1,C)=1 and leaves a->b with capacity 1 again. This repeats until the flow reaches its maximum of 2C, which takes 2C=200 iterations. Integer capacities only guarantee that the algorithm stops within (max-flow value) iterations, not within m. So the statement is false.
